title: How to prepare an electrical project brief
text: Planning guide · September27,2026  A useful electrical project brief tells the contractor what you want to achieve without trying to design the installation yourself.  Start with the outcome  Describe the spaces and how you intend to use them. Separate the essential work from optional additions. A short list of priorities is more useful than a vague request to upgrade everything.  Collect property information  Include the property type, city, occupancy and access restrictions. Gather any available drawings or photographs you already have; do not remove covers or inspect electrical equipment yourself.  Explain coordination and timing  Identify renovation stages, other trades and any landlord or strata requirements. Ask who will coordinate access, shutdowns and approvals rather than assuming these are included.  Ask for a written scope  Request a clear account of what is included, what is excluded, what needs a site visit and what could change the price. Keep the scope and subsequent changes in writing.   Prepare your project enquiry →

title: What to compare in electrical project quotes
text: Planning guide · September27,2026  Price matters, but two quotes may describe very different work.  Compare the same scope  Check each quote against your project brief. Look for differences in fixtures, equipment allowances, finishing work and disposal. Ask for clarification where descriptions are too broad to compare.  Understand responsibilities  Confirm who supplies materials, coordinates other trades, arranges access and handles required approvals. Ask how the contractor documents changes after work begins.  Discuss timing and payment  Ask about availability, project stages, payment terms and how unexpected conditions affect scheduling. Avoid assuming an enquiry or preliminary estimate is a confirmed booking.  Keep a decision record  Save the quotes and written answers together. Select a qualified contractor whose scope and responsibilities you understand. Sparkys currently offers planning resources rather than contractor verification or dispatch.
